questions.stem: Which four nerves does an axillary block of the arm target?
questions.answer: Musculocutaneous, median, ulnar and radial nerves

questions.stem: During an axillary block, which nerve is nearly always blocked although it is not aimed for?
Which three nerves are often missed by an axillary block?
questions.answer: Axillary, medial brachial cutaneous and intercostobrachial (T2) nerves

questions.stem: Where does an axillary block give full cover?
How can the medial upper arm (intercostobrachial, T2) be covered during an axillary block?
questions.answer: Subcutaneous injection just distal to the axilla

questions.stem: Which upper limb surgery is an axillary block indicated for?
When is an axillary block used instead of higher brachial plexus sites?
questions.answer: When higher sites are unusable, such as local infection, burns, indwelling venous catheters

questions.stem: Why does an axillary block have fewer serious complications than interscalene or supraclavicular blocks?
questions.answer: It is far from the lung and neuraxis

questions.stem: What is the main risk of an axillary block?
options: Intravascular injection into axillary artery or vein

questions.stem: Among upper limb nerve blocks, which has the slowest onset?
What needle length is used for an ultrasound-guided axillary block?
What local anaesthetic volume is typical in adults for ultrasound-guided axillary block?
How should the arm be positioned for an ultrasound-guided axillary block?
options: Adducted by the side of the body
Abducted to 90 degrees and externally rotated
Flexed above the head at 180 degrees

questions.stem: How deep are the structures of the axilla seen on ultrasound for axillary block?
On ultrasound, at which clock positions is the radial nerve reliably seen in the axilla?
What volume is used to hydrodissect around nerves in an ultrasound-guided axillary block?
What volume is injected posterior to the artery first, for the radial nerve in axillary block?
In an axillary block, why is the radial nerve injected before the median and ulnar nerves?
questions.answer: Median or ulnar injection first pushes structures deeper and hides them

questions.stem: In axillary block, after withdrawing almost to the skin, what volume goes to the median and ulnar nerves?
In an axillary block, what does stimulating the musculocutaneous nerve produce?
What is the single-injection alternative to targeting each axillary nerve separately?
questions.answer: Injection deep to the artery at 6 o'clock

questions.stem: Why should an axillary block be aspirated often and injected slowly?
questions.answer: Systemic toxicity has followed seemingly easy ultrasound-guided blocks

questions.stem: In axillary block, what does no visible spread on injection suggest?
questions.answer: The needle tip is in a vein

questions.stem: How often does the musculocutaneous nerve leave the median nerve below the axilla?
What are the two purposes of a continuous axillary catheter?
Which needle approach is used for a continuous axillary catheter?
For a continuous axillary catheter, how far is it threaded past the needle tip?
How is spread around the artery confirmed after a continuous axillary catheter is placed?
questions.answer: Inject local anaesthetic through the catheter

questions.stem: How does the long-axis view for axillary catheter placement compare with the standard approach?
questions.answer: Harder, and neither approach has been shown to be better

questions.stem: In the landmark (transarterial) axillary technique, what elbow position is used?
In the landmark (transarterial) axillary technique, where should the artery pulse be palpated?
questions.answer: As high in the axilla as possible

questions.stem: In the transarterial axillary technique, when should the needle stop advancing?
questions.answer: When blood can no longer be aspirated
